headline: The forgotten metropolis: Does Kolkata still stand a chance against India's booming cities?
lead: Kolkata was long the political and economic center of India. Today, the city has fallen behind metropolises like Delhi, Mumbai, and Bangalore in terms of development. However, it has preserved its cultural identity. A visit.
seo_title: Forgotten Metropolis: Does Kolkata still stand a chance against India's booming cities?
social_title: Kolkata has fallen behind in its development, but has preserved its identity.
print_subtitle: While other Indian cities are booming, Kolkata risks falling behind.
summary_bullets_en: Kolkata has preserved its character and charm despite historical setbacks and slower development compared to booming cities like Bangalore, remaining affordable and livable. However, it is increasingly being abandoned by young residents searching for better career opportunities elsewhere.

Politically, the city is dominated by the Trinamool Congress under Mamata Banerjee, while its secular left-wing tradition and cultural diversity are still evident but face increasing commercialization.
Kolkata struggles with infrastructure issues and a lack of economic innovation, yet its historical heritage is cherished and partially revitalized by residents.

original_de.headline: Die vergessene Metropole: Hat Kolkata gegen Indiens Boomstädte noch eine Chance?
original_de.lead: Kolkata war lange das politische und wirtschaftliche Zentrum Indiens. Heute ist die Stadt in der Entwicklung hinter Metropolen wie Delhi, Mumbai und Bangalore zurückgefallen. Ihre kulturelle Identität hat sie dafür bewahrt. Ein Besuch.

body.caption: In Kolkata, the pace of life is more leisurely than in other large Indian cities. In the evenings, people like to gather on benches in front of houses for tea.

body.text: A group of young people have gathered on the steps along the banks of the Hooghly River at dusk. The Hooghly is one of the Ganges' distributaries before the great river empties into the Bay of Bengal south of Kolkata. The brown water flows sluggishly past the steps, mosquitoes buzz in the air as daylight quickly gives way to darkness. «Kolkata is a slow city, it's not as hectic as Delhi, Mumbai, or Bangalore,» says Dipsita Dhar. «We love to take a nap after lunch. We're proud of that. But that also means everything takes longer here.»

The 32-year-old conducts research at the university on issues of labor, migration, and gender, and has long been active in local politics for the communists. She appreciates the leisurely pace of life in Kolkata. She also appreciates that life in the city is still relatively inexpensive. "Among India's major cities, Kolkata is the most affordable," says the young left-wing politician. "Kolkata remains a livable, inclusive city. Here you can still get a meal for 10 rupees and a decent room for 5,000 rupees." That's only 45 Swiss francs.

The downside, however, is that Kolkata has fallen behind other metropolises in its development. While Kolkata, with over 15 million inhabitants, remains India's third-largest metropolitan area after Delhi and Mumbai, Kolkata doesn't feature when discussing India's booming cities. While Bangalore, Chennai, and Hyderabad have developed into important technology centers, Kolkata seems to be stuck in a different era.
With the partition of India, Kolkata lost its hinterland

Calcutta, as the city was long known, was founded in 1690 by the British East India Company as a trading post on the east bank of the Hooghly River. Over the centuries, the city developed into the economic and political center of the British colonial empire. However, its decline began in 1911 when the capital was moved to Delhi. When India was partitioned in 1947, Calcutta's economic hinterland became part of East Pakistan, present-day Bangladesh.

body.caption: For decades the jute industry formed the economic backbone of Kolkata and West Bengal, but from the 1970s onwards a series of long strikes led to the decline of many factories.

body.text: The partition of India along religious lines drove millions of Hindus across the border into Kolkata in 1947. Many ended up in slums. When Bangladesh seceded from Pakistan in 1971 after a bloody war of independence, millions more Hindu refugees sought refuge in the city. In the 1970s, major strikes accelerated the decline of the jute industry, which had formed the economic backbone of the city. A long period of stagnation followed.

In 1985, then-Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi described Kolkata as a "dying city." The powerful labor movement hampered development, and the leftist policies of the then-ruling communists deterred investors. However, in the 1990s, economic liberalization brought a degree of growth to Kolkata. Rajarhat New Town, a modern satellite city for the middle class, was founded on Kolkata's eastern edge and is now considered an urban planning success. Since then, several IT companies have established themselves there. However, compared to booming cities like Bangalore, Kolkata's IT sector is developing only slowly.
Young people are leaving the city en masse

Many young people therefore see no future for themselves in Kolkata. "Living a comfortable, relaxed life – that's no longer enough for many in the younger generation," says Dhar. Kolkata used to be a preferred destination for migrant workers from other parts of India. Today, however, more people are leaving the city than moving there. University graduates, in particular, are finding it difficult to find a job in Kolkata after graduation, says Dhar. In their search for work, many are going to Bangalore and other large IT centers in South India.

Unlike many of her peers, Dhar has remained in Kolkata. The 32-year-old has made a name for herself as a student leader and is considered one of the rising stars of the left in West Bengal. She intends to run in the upcoming regional elections for the Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M). The party governed Kolkata and West Bengal continuously from 1977 to 2011. However, the era when communists dominated the region's political life is over.

Since 2011, Kolkata and West Bengal have been governed by the Trinamool Congress under Mamata Banerjee. The 70-year-old is combative and close to the people. Politically, she is difficult to categorize. However, she has a firm grip on her party and the state. She keeps voters loyal with a comprehensive welfare program. The communists' chances of gaining ground in the spring elections are therefore slim. Nevertheless, Dhar believes in her party and in the future of the city.
Caste and religion play hardly any role in politics

She is proud of Kolkata's left-leaning, secular tradition. The city's society is highly politicized, she says. Discussions are passionate, and everyone has an opinion on politics. However, the discourse is less about religion and more about social issues. Dhar appreciates that—unlike in many parts of northern India—caste and religion play only a minor role in politics. "None of our parties are based on religious identity. We don't have Hindu parties or Muslim parties," Dhar says.

Like most Bengalis, Dhar is also proud of the city's cultural heritage; with its numerous bookstores, theaters, and film festivals, Kolkata is considered the cultural capital of India. However, she is critical of how the past is romanticized. "We Bengalis are a nostalgic people," says Dhar. "We are proud of our past and love to revel in the glory of Rabindranath Tagore and others." But the younger generation is no longer content with that.

body.caption: The poet, musician, and polymath Rabindranath Tagore enjoys widespread veneration in West Bengal. His birthplace in Kolkata continues to attract many admirers.

body.text: The poet and polymath Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) is a giant of Bengali literature and played a crucial role in establishing Kolkata's reputation as a city of literature, music, and theater. His poems, songs, novels, and plays remain an integral part of the city's culture. However, Tagore's reputation is now so overwhelming that few other authors can rival it. Consequently, very little genuinely new work is being created in Kolkata.
The culture in Kolkata has become more commercialized.

Kolkata no longer lives up to its reputation as India's cultural capital, says Mahalaya Chatterjee, professor of urban economics. In the 1970s and 80s, Kolkata was an international city, engaged in exchange with the world. Today, however, it is very insular. The quality and character of its culture have changed. It is no longer a given that middle-class children learn music, dance, and poetry. This tradition is increasingly being lost, says Chatterjee.

She chose a park in the center of Kolkata for the interview. Across the street is a cultural center where the Kolkata Film Festival has just ended. Next door is the Academy of Arts, which hosts exhibitions, readings, and theatrical performances every evening. A few older people are waiting on chairs in the driveway for the show to begin. The younger people have made themselves comfortable on the lawns.

Kolkata still boasts a vibrant cultural scene. It's less elitist and exclusive than those in Delhi or Mumbai. Theaters attract not only the educated middle class but also the general public. However, according to Chatterjee, everything in Kolkata has become more commercialized. She says that the film festival used to primarily feature arthouse films. Now, however, it screens mainstream films from Mumbai, and Bollywood stars attend the opening.
The last word today rests with Mamata Banerjee

Chatterjee sees one reason for the decline of culture in Mamata Banerjee. The Chief Minister of West Bengal, while herself part of the old Bengali middle class, does nothing to preserve its culture. Instead, under her government, culture has become increasingly politicized, the professor criticizes. Banerjee also lacks a vision for the city. All power is concentrated in her hands, and all decisions are made by her. "The final word rests with her; her perspective is all that matters," says Chatterjee.

A common criticism is that while Banerjee champions the city's beautification, she does little to improve its often dilapidated infrastructure. Under Banerjee's leadership, the entire city was painted blue and white because she favors these colors. Bridge railings, government buildings, street curbs, park furniture: everything is blue and white. The colors lend the city a certain freshness. But otherwise, it bears the marks of time and the tropical climate.

body.caption: West Bengal's Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee has dominated politics in Kolkata for 14 years. Here she puts the finishing touches on a sculpture of the goddess Durga, who enjoys special veneration in the city.

body.text: Everywhere the plaster is crumbling, the colors are faded, the facades weathered. Unlike Mumbai, the skyline is hardly dominated by skyscrapers. Most of the buildings in the city center on the east bank of the Hooghly River are low. Alongside bicycle rickshaws, many of the old yellow taxis, which are among Kolkata's iconic symbols, still ply the streets. When the authorities decided last year to revoke the licenses of the oldest models, there were widespread protests. For many residents, these legendary taxis are a cultural asset worthy of protection.
Kolkata has retained its own character

Architect Ayan Sen sees it as a positive sign that the people of Kolkata value their cultural heritage. «We love to build new things, but we also love to restore and repurpose old buildings,» he says over morning coffee at the Tollygunge Club, an exclusive golf club in the south of the city. And there is much worth preserving. Kolkata was once known as the «City of Palaces» because so many wealthy landowners built themselves city palaces there. It also has a rich industrial heritage that can be repurposed.

Sen says that the renewal of many neighborhoods happened organically. It wasn't the city administration, but the residents themselves who revitalized their communities. He adds that the urban fabric is still intact, especially in the north. This part of the city was formerly known as Black Town, as it was home to Indians. To this day, it remains more densely populated and poorer. In contrast, White Town in the south was reserved for the British. It is better planned, with wider streets and more green spaces. Today, it is primarily inhabited by the middle class.

Today, India is at a crossroads where it must decide, says Sen. Does it want to tear everything down and rebuild like China? Or does it want to preserve its cultural heritage? The architect doesn't want to join in the lamentations about the city's decline. "I believe Kolkata is on the right track. I see its development very positively: not because Kolkata will become an economic powerhouse tomorrow, but because its quality of life will always attract people."

Kolkata appears less dynamic today than other Indian metropolises. However, it has managed to avoid some of the problems plaguing boomtowns. While real estate prices in Mumbai are skyrocketing, Delhi is shrouded in smog during the winter, and Bangalore is on the verge of gridlock, Kolkata remains affordable and livable. This slower pace of development has allowed Kolkata to preserve its character and charm. It would therefore be premature to write off this city on the Hooghly River entirely.
Contribution: Utsa Sarmin
